translations.text: Truly, those who love God and carry out his divine commandments are worthy of most beautiful, much-desired, divine praise and of a splendid encomium.
For our King and God himself calls them blessed in the commands of the Gospel, when he says:
"Blessed are the poor in spirit," and then, one after another, all the other beatitudes.
And at the end he sets before them something like a gift and a shining crown, grants it as the reward for their labours, and says to them:
"Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven." And in another place he says:
"Do not rejoice in this, that evil spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven."
And again David, the ancestor of God, says: "Therefore my heart rejoiced and my tongue sang," and "The dwelling of all who rejoice is in you."
This joy comes from that divine blessedness which the same prophet describes at the beginning of the Psalms as the blessedness of the man "who does not walk in the way of the ungodly," and again:
"Blessed are the blameless in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord." And Solomon, the all-wise son of an all-wise father, says:
"Blessed is the man who has acquired understanding, and the mortal who has found knowledge."
And Paul, the golden nightingale of the Church, cries out: "Rejoice always in the Lord; again I say to you, rejoice."
For your faith draws you toward eternal blessedness. And strengthened by this hope, the saints of the Old and New Law
learned patience, and by faith they ran toward the crown of the heavenly calling, as the same Paul, the mouth of Christ, says:
"For faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen; for by it the elders were attested." These are the ones who shone with divine radiance in the Old and the New.
For just as many gardens and orchards and a multitude of plants of every kind are watered from a single, richly flowing spring, so from that divine grace and gift
the distribution of graces is poured out on everyone, on each one individually, as the same Paul cries out:
"There are distributions of gifts," and various kinds of tongues. And again he says: "First apostles were appointed, then shepherds and teachers and fathers."
For, one generation after another, the grace of the Spirit does not cease to bring forth children of the baptismal font, as the word says:
"Make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; and behold, I am with you,"
and so on. And elsewhere: "Increase and multiply and fill the earth." And again the Apostle says:

"Jesus Christ, yesterday and today and the same forever." He has now caused the radiance of these new luminaries to shine out like the flash of the morning star in the new firmament of the holy Church,
so that they may shine like stars over the face of the whole world, and stir the hearts of all who are zealous to imitate their godly way of life.
For behold, by God's decree, new luminaries, guides and teachers have appeared in our times too, as Elijah and John did in the Old [Covenant],
And after them Paul of Thebes and the great Anthony, Macarius, Euthymius, Sabbas and Gerasimus — and why do we need to name each one individually? — all those who were like them and imitated them,
who walked with zeal the narrow and hard way that leads to the heavenly city, whose architect and maker is God.
But some say: "In these our times no one is any longer able to be like the first fathers, for by some divine dispensation this has been hidden [from us]."
But you, beloved, listen attentively [to the account of] him for whose sake this discourse is now set forth.
For in every respect the all-radiant, all-holy father and teacher, the blessed Serapion, worthy of heavenly rank, became like these holy fathers.
So we will tell some few things gathered from his life, narrating them in writing and recalling them to your holiness, who love to hear divine things,
O honorable and godly community, likened by your well-ordered standing to the ranks of heaven, who have been made dwellers in the tents [that were] the fruit of his labors,
priests and fathers of the great desert of Zarzma, to whom this great luminary father, teacher and instructor of fathers, fell as a good portion,
so that we may hear his teachings and his godly deeds and labors, and may glorify the Father in heaven, as the Lord says:
"Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works," and so on.
And it is fitting for us, brothers, that we too, according to our strength, should show that we imitate that great teacher and shepherd,
and now let us listen attentively and diligently to this small verbal portrait of his long and greatly desirable life, and of this present gathering here.
And I, this utterly unworthy one, beseech your love with tears that you may join in compassion for my weakness, so that a worthy word may be given at the opening
of my mouth by the Word who makes the speechless speak and strengthens the weak; for the discourse now begins with the beginning of his life.
This blessed and all-praised Serapion sprang up in the land of Klarjeti, from worthy parents who lived honorably and simply,
Those who were fed by labour and by working the land, and from their labour richly fed the poor,
and as far as they were able gave a helping hand to the helpless, and lived in meekness and humility, in keeping with the prophetic word:
"On whom shall I look, but on the meek and humble," and so on.
The father of this blessed one was called Cyprian, but we do not know the name of his mother — not because of any disgrace,
but because it has been hidden by time; for she who brought forth such fruit cannot have perished in disgrace and worthlessness, as the Lord also said:
"A good tree cannot bring forth bad fruit." So the mother of this blessed one was hidden from the world as regards the remembrance of her name,
for when she had brought this holy child into the light together with his two brothers, one of whom was older and one younger,
whom the discourse will mention many times — for when she had borne these three children and rejoiced in her childbearing, as the Psalmist writes,
"a mother rejoicing over children," she who had brought them into the light departed into the unfading light.
But the youngest son, John, remained wholly imperfect and tongue-tied. His father Cyprian raised him, as befits a father who loves his children.
But not many years afterward the father of these blessed ones also died. He passed away into the presence of God, enriched with a good old age.
And all three of the boys were left behind, cast into the flame of poverty like the boys of Babylon.
But here the narrative means to turn aside briefly to another matter, so that the fruit-bearing of those good plants may be shown all the more clearly,
and after this, how again they spread out with outstretched branches, not only a hundredfold but even more, thirtyfold, sixtyfold and a hundredfold,
so that at the end of the story you may understand how sweet and beautiful a cluster of grapes ripened from the labours of their teaching.
But now it is fitting for us to recall, concerning those great deserts and monasteries, where their building came from,
or who their builders were: first the Spirit and divine grace, and then the holy fathers who were moved by it.
For when the holy and great desert monastery of Opiza had been built by monks who were called Amona, Andrew, Peter and Macarius,

after this he came from there and, by divine instruction, built a small hermitage [?] and a gathering-place for a few brothers. He built it in a rocky place that people could not reach, which they call Parekhi.
And this account comes down to us from the fathers: Michael was the builder, a worker of lofty and great miracles and signs,
who was a disciple of the great Shio the wonderworker. Shio shone like the morning star in the land of Kartli.
The all-wise Serapion made his way to this blessed Michael, accompanied by a brother who was young in age.
For he entrusted himself to the great Michael as to a father of souls and a nurturer of orphans.
That blessed one also had many other disciples, perfect and radiant in virtue. Just as the great Anthony had Hilarion and Macarius, so Michael had Basil and Markelaoz.
And together with them he received the blessed Serapion and his brother and counted them among the company of disciples.
But the eldest brother, following worldly custom, took possession of the inheritance from his father. He likewise embraced a talent: caring for strangers and the poor.
After this, when the time came, our holy father, as one who was worthy, was perfected with the honour of the priesthood by Michael's command. He became a worthy servant of the divine altar.
And this most renowned Michael, the worker of great signs, raised them and led them up to perfection in virtue.
From there they saw his divine way of life, the richest rivers of his teachings, and the great signs and miracles he performed,
These things his disciples wrote down after his death. When the holy men saw all this,
they looked closely at good examples, like skilled painters, and by receiving the graces that came from him they built on the foundation of his teachings not hay and reed,
but gold, silver, and precious stones and carbuncles. And he loved them as men who received his teachings well.
In this way they spent a long time in his presence and became his imitators in everything.
But it is right for us to listen diligently to the rest of the story: how they came to the regions of the land of Samtskhe.
Let us tell it now. While that great father and teacher Michael was standing at his night prayer, a kind of ecstasy came over him. He was caught up to heaven and saw someone
beautifully dressed like a priest. This figure told him to send at once to the land of Samtskhe the disciples he had taught, who are Serapion and John.
He also showed him certain signs and images of the place they should go to. When they arrived, they would find
that sign, and there they were to begin building a monastery and to gather many souls in it to glorify God, the King of all. And let this be enough about the vision!
When the saint, who had seen many divine signs, came back to his senses, he called the holy men, and with a grieving face he said to Serapion:
"Beloved son, and brother in Christ, Serapion, this command has seemed very heavy to me,
for the soul dearly loves the companionship of those it was raised with, and even more of those who have been bound together by divine love.
"Now, since this command is from God, that you go out from here and build a monastery wherever God shows you,"
When he heard this from the saint, he fell at his feet and lay there for a long time without a word. But the saint took him by the hand, raised him up, and said to him:
"Take heart, son, for it is impossible to resist the divine command even a little. And this too is a command:
the one who told you only to carry the cross alone is the same one who now tells you to carry the living image of his incarnation, and so go out,
so that when you have built the holy church, you may set the icon up in it to be venerated, to drive away diseases and infirmities, and to redeem many souls."
When the holy man heard many such things, instead of words he poured out a flood of tears and said:
"Father, if it pleases you, pray to God for me that he not separate me from your holy community, or from always seeing your holy face."
But he answered him: "So that you do not fall short of the divine crown of the obedient, stop your objections from now on and get yourself ready to travel the roads.
Take your brother John and four of these brothers as your travelling companions." He also told them certain signs of that place,
so that they could easily recognize the place they had been commanded to build on, and he said this as well:
"Know, sons, that you will become the cause of eternal life for many souls, so that, as the Apostle says:
'At the sound of the trumpet you may stand before the King together with the many who have been saved through you.'"
When he heard such words from the saint, he no longer dared to object.
Instead he fell down before him in tears. The holy men embraced each other tenderly, and all the brothers did the same, and they took the saint's prayer as their provision for the journey.
When they set out, they carried with them the living icon of the Transfiguration, as a helper and a hope for all Christians.
On their journey they went along without hardship, as if they were walking through royal palaces, until they reached that mountain,
which rises as if to the height of heaven, and they stopped at the place called Bera's Cross.
The holy man had shown them the place where the monastery was to be built, pointing it out as if with his finger. When they came down to the end of the gorge,
which is [?] (utqwisa), they came to a place named Dzindze. They looked it over and examined it, and saw that it was a wilderness, shut in by forests and gorges.
and the brothers loved him. And the saint said to them:
"The signs that our teacher, who sent us out, told us about are not in this place."
Even so, they set to work and began to build a small hut and some place for a monastery, and they stayed there for many days.
But the lords of that village learned that some foreign monks wanted to build a monastery in that place,
and they did not want this. They were completely beastlike, irreligious and wicked, and they did not want the blessing of those holy men.
So they attacked them. It is written of the men of Nazareth that "they led Christ to the brow of the hill
on which their city was built." In the same way these holy men were driven to the bank of the river that lies to the east of that place.
They crossed that river and went about two miles to the west of it, into places that were all forest and impassable for people.
As they made their way through those narrow places with hardship and toil, they found the marks and signs that the great teacher had told them about, and they rejoiced with great joy.
They came to know with full assurance that the road they had travelled in hardship had not been useless or in vain.
They saw a small hill, higher than the places around it, and to the east of that hill a spring of water welling up, flowing and beautiful. It fulfilled the desire that had driven their journey.
They looked all around and examined the place, but no level ground was found that was wide enough to hold them.
The holy man ordered that a place be prepared between the spring and the hill and that a small hut be built there.
This hut would shelter them while they lived as strangers in a foreign land, and in it they could venerate the living icon.
Here let us turn our account and set out clearly for your love how that place came to prosper,
and who the man was who brought everything to a good end for them, as if by God's command.
There was a great and eminent prince in this land who surpassed everyone in wealth and in the number of his people and estates. His lands were wide and extensive.
He was rich not only in earthly and worldly things; he was also counted among all those who lived in the service of God.
As it is written of Job, he was "truly righteous and blameless." Such a man was he, and he lived in many palaces and tents.
His name was Giorgi, and he was also called Chorchaneli. His palaces were built in the districts of Chorchani and Zanavi.
Most of the time he would hunt in the places called Tskhrocha, because there were many goats and other wild animals there.
A house had been built in those parts, so that whenever night overtook them they would lodge in it, because of the darkness of night and because the dense forests were impassable.
And it happened that when the saints had encamped at the place mentioned above, they made a tent near that hill and kindled a fire, and a great quantity of smoke rose up.
When the faithful George saw it while he was out hunting wild game, he was greatly amazed and said to those standing before him:
"Where does this thick smoke in that place come from? Or who needs a fire there, and for what?
If someone is hunting game there, why has he become so bold and shameless? And even if someone needs it for some other purpose, how is it that we know nothing of it?"
But no one answered, so he at once ordered one of his servants: "Go quickly," he said,
"and find out exactly what this is about, and report to us: what is this thing we are seeing?"
The young man went at once and, with hardship and toil, followed the smoke of the fire.
When he arrived there, he saw the tent and men clothed in the strange cloaks of desert-dwellers. The man was startled, and they too were amazed.
The messenger asked who they were and what their business was, that they were seen in such poverty and in such a trackless place.
They answered him and said: "Friend, who are you, and why do you need to know exactly about our situation?" And the man said to them:
"I belong to a great prince whose name is George. He sent me, because he was amazed to see the smoke of a fire, and that there were people at all, in a place like this."
When the saint heard that he was a ruler and lord of those places, he asked in detail about all his affairs.
When he learned for certain that he was lord of those places and held all those districts, the holy Serapion immediately began and recounted to him everything from the beginning up to that time:
for what reason they had come to that place, and that he intended to build a monastery. And he added this as well:
"It is a divine command, and we are disciples of Michael of Parekhi, who is made radiant by signs and miracles."
When the man had heard all this, he reported everything, along with what he had seen, to the great ruler and to all those standing before him.
They, together with the ruler, were seized with fear and amazement and thought the matter something marvellous. And the man said to them:
"I have seen men who are entirely in the flesh, in the form and appearance of monks, and not as some apparition, but plainly."
When day dawned, the ruler again commanded two of his own close attendants, men who were also prudent of mind, to find out everything exactly. And those men set out.
When they arrived before the holy father, he saw them and understood that they were nobles and close attendants of the great ruler.
The saint went out to meet them, greeted them warmly, and sent them before the icon. When they had venerated it, they received a blessing and rejoiced very greatly.
Then those nobles said to the holy Serapion and to the other brothers:
"We thank God, holy lords, who in these times has looked upon us and shown us heavenly men on earth.
But now satisfy us: for what reason has your holiness seen fit to come to these trackless and impassable places?"
Then the holy father Serapion made the sign of the precious cross, sighed from the depth of his soul, and said to them:
"Beloved ones, although we are sinners, we are Christian men,
and we believe in Christ God, who became man for our life, and we await the resurrection of all and the blessedness prepared for the saints.
We say nothing outside the truth, for we are disciples of the great and renowned Michael of Parekhi, and we were sent out by him at a divine command,
so that we might build in this place a gathering place for rational sheep." And he told them everything in order, one thing after another.
When they understood that their words were true and heard the name of that great teacher, they bowed down before the living icon,
greeted the saints, and set off. They hurried to tell the God-serving Giorgi everything they had seen and heard.
When he heard that they were disciples of Michael, he believed that their words were true and rejoiced. He went to his house and longed to see them.
After three days he ordered that the roads leading to the place where the saints were be made ready. He made himself ready and took some small eulogia (blessing gifts)
suitable for those desert-dwelling men, and he took priests with him as well, with censers and incense.
He sent swift runners ahead of him to prepare the roads. And they hurried on to the place where the saints were.
When the saints learned of this, they went out at once to meet the ruler, and they went out to the place where the spring is,
where he got down from his horse and fell down before the living icon. In the same way he greeted the saints and was blessed by them.
Then the ruler answered those blessed fathers and spoke to them with a fervent spirit:
"I give thanks to God and King, O holy ones, who did not disregard our unworthiness and worked a miracle with me in my days,
who has now made me, utterly unworthy as I am, worthy first to venerate his living icon, and then your holy faces."
Then the blessed Serapion was filled with the Holy Spirit, and like a river he poured forth divine teachings from his honey-dripping tongue,
And like the river of Eden, a golden stream flowed out from his mouth, so that the prince and everyone standing before him were amazed. Because of this they fell at his feet and said to him:
"Christ has sent you to us like one of the apostles. Now then, father, command us to do what is right!"
And the saints told him, as far as they were able, not to delay the divine command, since it was fitting to build a monastery in this place for the gathering of God-loving souls.
But the ruler fell down before them and said to them: "I beg you, O holy ones, do not lay a heavy request upon me,
for behold, you see how utterly useless and unworkable this place is, and I see you wholly without means, like the apostles.
Yet since God has sent you as labourers for me, these works you speak of will not succeed without me.
Now there is a place that is suitable and fit for these works, wherever your holiness may command,
so that we may build the monastery there, for here it is utterly impossible to do anything of the kind."
But the holy man said to him: "God, who commanded Moses to part the sea with a rod, and again in the desert to make water spring up from a waterless rock,
and who rained manna on the people when they needed food — that same God is here as well, and he has made hard things easy through your arrangement and through divine help.
But it is impossible for us to oppose the divine command and exchange this place for another, for signs and revelations bear witness to this place."
The prince said to him: "Is it right, father, for a man to give himself up to hardships of his own will, and in the end be found reproached and worn out for nothing?"
The holy man said to him: "Listen wisely to this parable, O prince. When pearls and precious stones lie scattered about, mixed in with the earth,
they do not shine before the eyes of those who love to look at them the way they do once they have been dug out, cleaned, and set in goldwork by good smiths.
Only then does their brilliance appear, and their workmanship and beauty become manifest. In the same way, when skilled workmen set their hands to this place,
then the eyes of those who see it will behold the beauty of this place. Therefore do not compel us to leave this place and exchange it for another, for we cannot do this."
When the prince heard this, he bowed his head and fell silent. After this he stood up, prayed, and said to them:
"Pray for us, holy ones, for I do not begrudge you this place. But to show compassion and help in any other way is completely impossible."
They brought him his horse and he left. He spoke to the holy ones, saying, "It seems I was not worthy of your prayer," and he went away grieving.
When he came to the river that lay in front of them, he saw a small rock, got down onto it, and sat down.
He called one of the young men and said to him: "Go, brother, and tell the holy ones to come to this place."
When he had sent him off, he said to his own people:
"Since the holy men did not want that place of Zanavi, where we might have built a great and lofty monastery, what should be done now?"
They said to him: "That we should not stand in the way of their zeal."
The prince said: "This matter does not come from men without the guidance of divine power. Therefore it is right for us to give help as far as we are able."
When the holy ones reached that place, the prince spoke to them again:
"I beg you, holy ones of God, grant me one thing. There are many good places, well provided with buildings. Go and see them,
"And if it pleases your souls greatly, here are lands and revenues and everything needed, in abundance." But the blessed Serapion said to him again:
"Like the apostle I would say: 'Even if an angel were to bring us good news other than what we have rejoiced in, we would not believe it.'"
Then Giorgi called a certain man who was young in years and [?] in strength, and said to him:
"Beloved son, go with these holy ones. Tomorrow, from dawn until evening, whatever area they walk around I have given to them, since they desire this place.
And if anyone is found harming them because they are strangers, let everyone know that they are building the monastery freely and as they wish, within our domain."
And he said to the holy fathers: "Take heart, for I will help you and look after you with all my strength,
and no one in these places that you intend to take as your own is against us. After three days I will see you again, if the Lord wills."
At this the holy men rejoiced greatly and gave thanks. And the fathers spent that night on the rock.
This report that has come down to us is also true: that night he saw a vision of an angel, which strengthened him and commanded him to work with diligence.
Because of this, two days later the holy man made two crosses with his own hands and set them up on that rock in the name of the holy archangels.
Later a small chapel was also built there, because signs and healings of the sick took place through the divine grace of the holy archangels.
But let us go back to the earlier account and keep to the order of the story as far as we are able.
When they had passed that night and the sun was rising, the holy man got up, along with his brother John and one of the brothers
(there were six of them in all). The three set out with the young man, and three were left behind at that place.
They began to walk along the bank of the river toward the west. As they went on, they reached the place where the two waters meet.
There was a mill there, a kind of house at that meeting point between the waters, which was called Sadzmo.
In it lived some wicked men, completely like beasts, as people of an uninhabited and foreign place are.
When we reached that place, the young man, our guide, said to us: "Holy men of God, which way do you want to go?"
We wanted to go all the way around the edge of those places and mark out their boundary, so we turned our faces southward to follow one of the rivers upstream.
But when the men of that mill-village saw us, they began to block our way and ran out ahead of us like rabid dogs.
The young man held them back and rebuked them angrily. The holy man also turned to them and spoke angrily in prophecy:
"I saw the ungodly man raised up as high as the cedars of Lebanon, and I passed by, and his place was not found."
But you, beloved, see how full of the divine Spirit this holy man was, and what he was foretelling for those men with that prophetic word:
namely, that after a short while they would be destroyed and would disappear completely from their place. In a little while, beloved, time [?] and the story will show you this.
But now let us go back to telling the earlier account. We went up along the bank of that river and reached a deep and [?] gorge, which is called Goderdzi's gorge.
We got into it with great difficulty, and because it was so thickly overgrown, for a long time we could not see the sky or the rays of the sun.
Because of this we were slowed down by hardship and toil, and we came out as if born out of a thick haze or out of the depths of [?],
when we climbed up to the head of that gorge and saw some small fields and a small village.
Right away a good man, an elder, came to meet us. He greeted the holy man warmly and urged him to rest a little from his labor,
because news of our coming had been heard throughout all those districts. The man asked us why we needed to travel through such pathless and impassable places.
The young man recognized him and told him all our affairs in full detail.
And the man begged us many times to spend that night at his house.
The saint thankfully accepted his good intention, asked his name, and said to him:
"It is impossible for us not to go to that place at this time." And the man said to him:
"My name is Ia. But your going to the place you speak of is [?] delayed for you." Then the saint said to him:
"Beloved brother Ia, take this labour upon yourself for God's sake and be our fellow traveller for a little while."
They brought a little bread, salt and cheese, and those who wished ate. But the saint did not taste anything at all.
And the man Ia became our fellow traveller. We set out toward the east and went over certain high ridges that were wooded and rocky.
When we had climbed to the highest places, the saint asked the man: "Beloved Ia, what is this place called?"
He told him: "This is a gathering place of the wild animals of the field, and it is called Bakta [the Pens]."
Then the saint took an iron double axe in his own hand and carved crosses on some very large rocks, which can be seen to this very day.
The saint looked again and saw, toward the east on that ridge, a lake stirred up with [?] (lali), which looked like smoke.
We were greatly amazed and asked the man: "What is this place of strange water?" And Ia answered us:
"This is a very deep lake called Satakhve ('the lake of the wild goats'). In it there is a multitude of wild goats and other beasts, and it is the mother of disturbances and fighting,
because at this season hunters of wild animals are seen here, gathered from every district, and they pursue one another over wrongful matters and are ready even to kill each other."
As we set out toward that lake, the man Ia fell down before the saint and gave thanks to God for having seen us.
And he told us that we should command him in everything, if we wanted anything from him.
The saint said to him: "Do not go away yet, brother, for this young man does not know these places."
And Ia said: "May Christ grant me to be always with your holiness, father."
When we had gone down to the shore of the lake, we asked the man the time of day. He answered us: "It is evening and the day is declining."
The saint answered: "What lies beyond these wooded ridges, or the height of this great mountain
which is above us?" He answered: "This mountain is high, the head of all these ridges, and it is called the Head of the Woods;
for it is the head of all these forests, and that is why it is called Sheshistavi [Head of the Woods]. Because of its height, people and animals cannot travel on it.
Ahead of us are places with few people. And now, since you are in a hurry to reach that place, Drosi [?], you should not delay,
so that night does not overtake you at a bad time." So the saint wished us to pass the lake on our right and go by the ravines that were in front of us.
As we were going, suddenly some wicked men came up and told us to stop going in the direction we were heading,
"For it is the season of the wild animals that come to this lake, and the hunters are ready in these places, so their hunt must not be thrown into confusion by you."
And they would not let us go toward those parts at all. The young man, our teacher, strongly resisted them, but they would not listen,
and instead they turned us back. We crossed the shore of the lake on the western side and came to the top of the descent from the ridge, where there was no trace of a track at all, and no road.
But that man Ia pointed out a small village to us. He named a respected and good man there, called Garbanel, and said to us:
"Go to that place by this narrow path, and that man will easily lead you to the place from which you can cross at dawn."
But, beloved brothers and fathers who listen eagerly, it is all the more fitting for us
to listen to these wonderful deeds and to glorify God, who granted us such a father and teacher.
When we came to the place they call Babgen and saw a small plain at the place called Bobkha, Ia told us everything about that man Garbanel.
Then Ia fell down before the saint and greeted him warmly. The saint made the sign of the cross over him and said to him:
"May God reward you for your journey, brother! And I tell you that soon you will see the punishment of those wicked, strife-loving men."
When he had parted from us and gone away, we went down that steep slope like a torrent of water.
As we came to the village, there was the man mentioned above, going to his house with his two sons.
When he saw the state we were in, he was startled. He questioned us kindly and looked us over.
He learned that we were the ones who had come to these places to build a monastery, and he saw
that our clothing no longer even looked like clothing and that our limbs were torn all over. Then, weeping, he embraced the holy man and kissed his feet.
When the holy man saw how that man acted, he said to him: "Beloved Garbanel, my brother in Christ,
now, please, show us a little compassion and help us on our journey: guide us as far as the river that lies to the north of us."
And he said earnestly and with tears:
"That cannot be, O holy one of God, for behold, at sunset God has brought you to your sinful servant,
"I see the wounds on your feet. I beg you to rest a little from the weariness of your journey, and I want to learn exactly
what this great fervour of your soul is, that has driven you to risk your life by travelling these [?] and impassable roads."
The holy man said to him: "It is impossible for me not to go to that appointed place."
But the man ran into the house and came out again with his wife. Like the widow of Zarephath and the Shunammite woman, they fell at the holy man's feet.
When they could not persuade him, the young man, our teacher, fell before his brother John and said:
"Look, we have no strength left in us. Let us do what this man says, because it is no longer the time for travelling."
But the saint said to him: "He who at Gibeon made the sun stand still for Joshua son of Nun, and again for the holy elder Bessarion,
this same one has made us worthy as well to see and venerate his holy icon while this sun is still up."
Then the man led them out, and as they were setting out, the young man said to the saints:
"Pray for me, holy ones, for tomorrow, if God wills, I will come to your holy feet." This happened by divine providence,
so that he would be a fellow witness of the glorious miracle that will be told shortly.
As we went on, we found a path in front of us that was narrow and hard to get through.
The man from Garbani ordered his son to go with us as far as the edge of the river. We went down into it, and as we were coming up again, the brothers saw us and came out to meet us.
But you, beloved, consider this wonder: from the time we left the man until we arrived,
the sun again stood still in its place, as the saint had said. We marveled at this and glorified God, [who glorifies] those who glorify him.
When the brothers who were there saw us, they wept over us, because our clothes were completely gone and our feet were torn and cracked.
We were comforted a little with the food that was found among them. When dawn came, we offered prayers, and the saint took wood with his own hand,
and, as we said before, he made crosses and set them up in the name of the holy archangels.
At about the third hour, while we were praying at that place, there came that man from Garbani and the youth,
our guide, together with two men who were strangers, and they hurried up to us. When we saw them, we rejoiced.
But they were gripped by some great fear, and the two strangers looked like dead men.
We asked them why they had come sighing and anxious, and who the men were who were voiceless and speechless like the dead.
Then the man of Garbani began to tell his story and said to the saints:
"When you set out, this young man was very tired, and it was night. We took food, and we greatly marvelled at your courage, and we glorified God and went to sleep.
When dawn came, we were getting ready to come to you.
Suddenly there was a shaking and a roaring, like a wind, and we were greatly astonished. A little later these men came,
as you see, and could barely speak. When we asked them, 'What was this noise and shaking?'
they answered and told us: 'The rock that stood west of the lake has split open, and its muddy waters have poured out. And we,
who happened to be around that place, scattered in great terror and came down to this man, because we knew him.'"
And while they were saying this, the river could be seen bearing witness to their words, because its banks could no longer hold it,
for the mud had overflowed on every side like [?], and because of this astonishment seized us all.
And the young man said to the saint: "Behold, I see that your words are deeds, for I remember yesterday, when you told the man
who had been our fellow traveller as far as the lake of Satakhi [?] that you would soon see the retribution of these men who love strife, and also of those men
who ran ahead of the reservoir of water like men possessed by demons. For I think that not even a trace of that place will be found."
And when the flooding of that river subsided, we learned the truth: the place where the lake had been now looked like a stony plain,
and the site of the mill-houses had also been overturned and had disappeared. After this the young man fell down before the saint, received his blessing, and said to him:
"If the Lord wills, I will see you soon. But if you want anything from the ruler, command me, for he too wishes to see you soon." And the saint said to him:
"Apart from a divine blessing, we presume to ask for nothing before him, for he himself knows everything better, according to the word of Solomon:
'The ears of the wise are always ready for divine words.'" And the young man left, and we remained in that same place.
And when the young man reached the prince, he told him everything in order. Those who heard it were overcome with amazement, terror seized them, and they glorified God.
Then that servant of God was filled with fear and joy, and he set out to see those miracles and signs, together with all his subjects and the people of the surrounding districts of those regions
who had heard of this great wonder. At once a great crowd gathered at the place where the saints were.
And when the prince arrived, he kissed the life-giving icon, greeted them by prostrating himself, and asked in amazement about the miracles.
And he learned everything in detail from the men who had been sent to him:
how the place of that lake had become a plain and the reservoir of water had been covered with sand and stones. The men who had escaped from that disaster told this themselves.
Then priests and monks came from each of their places and joyfully greeted the saints. Many other monks also gathered.
And from that place on the riverbank we went up, with prayer and litany, to the hill mentioned earlier.
And by the prince's command the place was prepared and levelled.
Other princes of the surrounding regions also arrived, and each of them told the saints how suitable their lands were for monasteries. And also the man
who had earlier driven them out of the place called Dzindze fell down fervently before them and urged them to build there. The saint answered him and said:
'The fear of God will not dwell in a wicked soul.' Nor is it right to cast pearls before swine, for even a blind man passes by gold lying in front of him.
But may your former error be forgiven. As for us, let no one compel us to move to another place." And the whole assembly loudly exclaimed:
"These miracles are comparable to those done by Moses, the parting of the sea and the springing up of water from the rock, and again to the parting of the Jordan by means of the Ark,
the parting of the Jordan, and again to the drying up by Gregory the Wonderworker of that lake which was the cause of enmity between the brothers.
In the same way this lake, the cause of disturbances and murders, has been dried up by these saints." But the saint, being a stranger to boasting, answered and said to them:
"Do not think, rulers and people, that these miracles were done by any power of ours. Rather, Christ God has glorified the image of his own face,
so that you may believe that these works which you see are not false and vain."
From then on the place was given a name that matched these events. The people who had been seized with dread and fear beyond words called it Zarzma.
They spent that night in prayer and psalm-singing. At dawn they took leave of the saints and went home with joy.
But George, the servant of God, stayed with them. He told them to look for a place where they wanted to build a church, and he gave them generously what they needed.
As he was leaving, he told them that there would be another visit. From then on they began to search for a place where they could build a church to the glory of God.
The saint wished to build a church on the highest hill. But his brother John and the other brethren said to him:
"No, holy father, not in this place, for it is high and cold, and these brethren are naked and poor." Because of this a dispute arose among them.
And just as Gideon laid out the fleece to test the matter, and again as the great Theodosius sought out a place by means of coals,
where he should build a monastery. These blessed men did the same: they filled two lamps with equal amounts of oil and set them in the two places under dispute.
There was a small ravine to the south of the highest place. John himself set John's lamp there, and holy Serapion set his on the hill.
Both of them stood in prayer. When day broke, Serapion's lamp was seen to have gone out, while John's lamp kept shining until midday.
This was a divine dispensation, so that the cathedral would be built on that high place not in haste but very beautifully, in its own time.
When everyone saw this, they agreed that they should begin building the church there.
the saint said to his brother with his honey-dripping tongue:
"Brother John, God has shown you this glorious wonder, because he saw the weakness of your understanding.
"But know this: after a short time a very beautiful cathedral will be built in this place."
They prepared the place, and the number of brethren grew, because the fame of that man of God drew people to him. They were watered by his sweet words as if by a river.
The man of Garbani mentioned earlier, and the two brothers who had escaped drowning in the lake, were tonsured as monks by the hand of the saint.
This new Moses had been commanded to lead the new Israel, so he needed a new Bezalel and Eliab as helpers in the work of his tabernacle.
He did not enter the cloud and receive the stone tablets on which the law and the commandments were written.
Instead, he carried in his mind their Writer himself, the One who spoke to that same Moses as he hid in the cleft of the rock: "I am who I am."

This same One talked with Moses and Elijah on Mount Tabor, with the chief disciples present. Here he is depicted in the flesh, and the saint carried him on his shoulders and set him up for the faithful to venerate.
For this reason they began to build the church, and they laid the foundation in the place that Ioane had chosen.

But building it became difficult, because the stones of those places were covered by forests. So they managed with great effort to get some from the water, and brought out from there some poor, unsightly stone.
The master builder and overseer of that work was Garbaneli, together with the two brothers.
When word spread that such men were building a church in this way, people began to come to the work on the church like a river.
But stone was not to be found anywhere, and they brought it from the river with hardship and toil.
Then the God-serving Giorgi came there again and looked over all their work. He was anxious that the church should be built well, and it came into his heart, and he said to those holy men:
"Fathers made wise by Christ, if it pleases your holiness, there is a place where its church has fallen in an earthquake.
Now, if you give the order, it is easy for us to bring that." When the holy men learned that the church was lying unused, they ordered that the work be undertaken quickly.
And at once they began to bring as much as was needed for the church.
Those stones can be recognized in some of the corners and vaults. The name of that place is Umts'a, and it is twelve miles away.
After three years the church was completed and adorned with every furnishing that was fitting for that time.
In it they set up the life-giving icon of the Transfiguration. After this the brothers also built cells for themselves.
A great community of brothers gathered, for the grace of the Spirit and the renown of that man of God drew everyone, since the Lord says:
"Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them."
How much more so among many gathered for the service of God!
The God-serving Giorgi provided all the necessities: mules, guards [?], and whatever the multitude of brothers needed.
And the holy one established the orders and canons of the church, through which they were watered with divine grace.
For this reason George, that man of God, also gave villages. He was so eager that he wanted to spend everything on that place, and many began to imitate him.
And just as long ago, for the tabernacle of Moses, [people offered] gems and pearls and the other materials for building the tabernacle,
so in the same way they presented offerings, each according to his means, for this new tabernacle, which is the Church of Christ.
Here the style of the account changes, in order to speak more fully of the miracles of this holy man, and so that the life of the God-serving Giorgi may also be revealed more clearly.
This was told to us not by obscure men, but by very distinguished and illustrious ones.
We mean Giorgi, bishop of Mtsqueri, who sprang from the gorge of Shuartkhli, from noble and God-fearing parents,
and was brought up in the famous desert monastery of Opiza. For that God-clothed man said with his truthful mouth:
"When I was in the desert monastery of Opiza, the dwelling of the holy Forerunner, John the Baptist, I went up from there to the great father Mikael, and when I was with him,
Then Michael sent out two of his disciples and wrote a letter to Serapion and to his brother John, telling them to come to him quickly,
for he knew the time of his own departure. He wanted them to see one another, and he wanted to learn in full detail how the building of that place, revealed from heaven, had come about.
And Serapion, obedient to his teacher's command, came quickly with his brother, and many other brothers were with him.

When the great Michael and Serapion saw one another, they rejoiced, as is fitting, with gladness mingled with tears. They gave thanks to God, and all the brothers received a blessing from one another.
When two days had passed and we had rested, on the third day the great Michael began to ask about the progress and condition of that place, and about who had been their helper and fellow laborer.
And the blessed Serapion began from the beginning and told him everything:
how the great prince George Chorchaneli had become their helper, and everything that had happened to them, and how in that place the multitude of brothers [?],
and about the great miracles of the drying up of the lake and of the hiding of those disobedient men, and everything that had taken place, one thing after another.
At this the holy man rejoiced, gave thanks to God, and blessed that blessed man George Chorchaneli;

and he also heard how the people had given the place the fitting name Zarzma because of the wondrous miracles that had struck them with terror. When the holy man heard all this, he rejoiced in spirit.
After this, Father Michael called the cellarer and told him to prepare supper.
Then at the ninth hour they recited the appointed psalms and sat down to supper. They [?] wine, and they mingled spiritual and bodily joy.
Then the holy father Michael, made radiant by great signs and miracles, looked at the blessed Serapion and said to him:

"O beloved son and brother Serapion, I truly believe in the miracles of God that have been accomplished through you. But as to how the prospering of that place will turn out, I will be fully assured if this comes to pass."
Now by divine providence there was on the wall of the church a palm branch that had been there for many years.
Father Michael took it with his own hand, gave it to the holy Serapion, and said to him:
"Son, plant this near the church. If it turns green, know for certain that it means that place will be fruitful.
Go, and build diligently." At this, amazement seized everyone sitting there, and they said to one another:
"Is not the greatness of the miracle great through both of these men?" But Serapion, who was wholly free of pride, fell down before the holy man and said to him:
"Holy one of God, nothing is impossible before you, for you have received power even to move mountains."
And he took it from his hands and planted it in the ground. After a little while it turned green, and by spreading out its branches it proclaimed that glorious miracle.
When everyone saw it, they were amazed and glorified God.
When news of this miracle spread through the surrounding deserts, everyone was astonished and gave glory to God, the worker of wonders.
Then one miracle followed another, which it is fitting to tell before returning to the proper bounds of our account.
For while they were still together like this for some time, joyful in spirit and in delight, and all were filled with divine grace,
One day, while he was praying at the third hour, a trance suddenly came over the holy man, and he stood for a long time in amazement.
After this, like someone woken from a deep sleep, he looked at the blessed Serapion and said to him:
"Hurry, brother, and go to the places where you have laboured, for certain disturbances are about to happen for some time."
"But if God wills, they will soon be dispelled. You will never see me again in this world, though, for I will soon depart from here."
"But at the gathering of all, by the will of God, I will see you joyful and radiant, like a good labourer made rich with his reward."
"And let your brother John go to another place. When it becomes known, the men he finds in that place, where he is to build a monastery, will eagerly become his fellow helpers in building it."
And he gave him a sign and a token of the place where John was to go.
Having spoken this sweet last charge and told them beforehand everything that was to come, he sent them away. They were full of tears, all the more because they had no hope of seeing him again.
When they reached the great desert of Klarjeti, at Opiza, the fathers came out to meet them, greeted them warmly and with longing, and showed them fitting honour.
And when they had spent some days
Since the holy man was humble and without arrogance, he could be seen with a sweet and [?] hand, standing with the builders of the church.
For along with his other virtues he was learned in the canons of the Church and greatly adorned with the rank of the priesthood.
So a certain man, gripped by arrogance and insolence, saw him in this guise and began to revile the holy man, saying:
"Look at the great and famous Serapion, how wordless and voiceless he appears! This man is not at all worthy of such honours."
While that man, filled with devilish envy, was saying this — behold your wonders, O Christ! — the word of the prophet was fulfilled, which says:
"The Lord will repay them for their lawlessness," and again: "Let the deceitful tongue be struck dumb, which speaks lawlessness against the righteous."
As they were standing in the church, that man suddenly fell down in front of everyone and lay there without a voice. His tongue hung out, swollen, and he [?] terribly and rolled about.
Then amazement seized all the choirs of chanters. Those who had heard what that man had said about the holy man said to one another:
"Perhaps this swift rebuke came upon him because of that holy man." Then the man came to his senses and understood his error. Although he could not speak with his tongue,
even so he fell down before the company of the fathers and confessed his error in front of them.
Then all of them fell down before the holy man, begging him to forgive that sin. And he spoke to them like this:
"Holy assembly and chosen company, far be it from me to think that anything has happened to this brother because of me. Rather, according to the word of James the apostle:
"'It befits us, in brotherly love, to pray for everyone,' and the Lord will grant relief to this sick man."
Then all of them fell down before this holy man even more earnestly: "Forgive him, holy one of God, and have mercy on this pitiable man."
The holy man said: "See, I too am ready, together with you." And he bent his knees and said:
"Lord Jesus, Son of God the Father, who came into the world to seek those who had gone astray: just as by a word you made the deaf and mute man speak,
in the same way, O King, Lord God, heal this youth as well, who has gone astray through the wickedness of the devil."
As soon as he had said this, the great violence of the youth's tongue subsided at once, and he was restored to his proper state.
Those who saw it were amazed and glorified God.
And this miracle became known to everyone, and they said:
"He who made the dry palm branch put out leaves, like the withered hand that the Lord healed,
and like the rod that blossomed for Aaron, and again like the tree that became green and at once bore fruit when the great martyr Charalampus leaned on it,
and again like Gregory, the light of the people of Agrigentum: the miracles now performed by the holy Serapion are in no way lesser than those miracles.
For the Lord says: 'Whoever believes in me will do greater works than mine,' and God is wonderful among his saints."
All of them said these and similar things to one another and glorified God.
From here let us take up the rest of the narrative again and return to our earlier account. When the saint had performed these miracles in those places
where he had been brought up, in the presence of his teacher, who was the head and guide of all his deeds, and in the presence of their elder brother, whom we mentioned earlier,
they saw him and greeted him with longing, and he lived among them for his whole stay there. Then they parted from the holy ones of that desert, took leave of the holy fathers and departed.
And when they had crossed the mountain called Arsiani and came to the Qveli gorge,
something happened there too, by providence, to make up what was lacking [271,13]. For behold, some men who were monks came to meet them and said to them:
"Welcome, divine labourers in the vineyard of Christ! It has been ordained that a monastery be built by you in these places,
a monastery we too have been working toward. We have been waiting for you, since we were told you would come. For here too it is you who are the leaders and teachers of this work."
They showed them the place where the signs had been seen, in accordance with the command of the great Michael.
Holy Serapion ordered his brother to begin diligently and build the monastery in accordance with the saint's command.
This greatly grieved John, but he did not dare to oppose the command of the two of them. He said only this to Serapion:
"If it is permitted for me to see your divine face from time to time, I am ready to carry out your commands."
The saint ordered that they should by all means see one another. The monastery was built in accordance with the command of the great teacher.
He adorned it with every adornment, as was fitting, and gave it the name of his namesake, for the place is called Saint John.
From time to time he would come to his brother and learn the whole rule of the monastery.

But here we have moved the rest of the account out of its order, because one account had become mixed with another, and we could no longer keep separate the building of the monastery that was built in John's name.
When holy Serapion had left there and come to his own community, everyone came to meet him with joy and greeted him with longing,
He looked them over and saw how much the new master builder had built, and how the multitude of brothers had grown into a great multitude. When he saw all this, he rejoiced and gave thanks to God.
But here the narrative must turn back again to another matter.
For they told the God-clad father Serapion of the death of the great prince George, who had been the builder of that place.
When he heard this, he mourned greatly, as was fitting. He wept as the Saviour wept over Lazarus, and all the more because he had not been present at his death.
So he told the steward, the priests and all the brothers that the next day they should go to his grave, at the place of Zanavi,
where a beautiful monastery stands built, whose first builders were Amaspo and Kurdia.
And now again, George's sister, who was the wife of the great prince Mirian, son of Beshken Bahlaundi, son of John; but George was bereft of children and childless.
For his two children had died in their infancy, and after them their mother too, who had brought them into the light, passed away; and he never again undertook to be joined to another wife.
And as we said, when the all-blessed George passed away, everything that he had,
his patrimony, all the churches and his possessions, he entrusted to his sister and assigned as their own property to her sons, who were called Sula, Beshken and Laklak.
And as we said, the saint went to his grave and wept over it bitterly and with compassion.
And, as was proper, he visited and consoled his sister Latavri, who was afterwards called Thecla,
and with a divine blessing he blessed all three of those youths, like the three youths of the line of Abraham.
Then he took the testament of the great prince George and read it, filled with tears. He prayed for him and blessed that blessed man,
for he had given everything richly and generously: estates with exemption from obligations, goods of many kinds, and a multitude of mounts and [?].
And with hope he commended the soul of that holy man. Meanwhile the years passed, and that place grew and advanced greatly.
But now that we have come to this point in the narrative, it is right to listen with understanding to what graces the great father Michael had been made worthy of. For behold, the place
about which the blessed Serapion had foretold, "Troubles and temptations are going to befall this place of your labours" – behold, let us now relate it.
That place was in great tranquillity and peace after the death of the great prince George, and his whole domain was prospering well,
which had been left to his sister Thecla and her sons. Then, through the snares of the devil, an unlawful strife arose, for Laklak killed his own sister's son.
For he said with force, "Give a share of the patrimony along with you to this sister of yours, since you also hold it through your mother."
Because of this, disputes multiplied between them, and so he killed his sister's son. After this had happened, the affair dragged on for three years.
But in the fourth year of these events God made illustrious the great high priest George of Shuartqali,
who occupied the see of Atskuri, for it was not right for the lamp to be hidden under a bed.

And when he had taken the governance of Samtskhe into his hands, he brought peace to his whole dominion, as was right, and took possession of all the estates and churches of those earlier troublemakers.
But the place called Zarzma stayed completely undisturbed, through the help of God and through the grace of father Serapion, who was clothed with signs through his miracles.
And when seven years had passed, all the disturbances and disorders were calmed and silenced by this holy prelate George.
Now the mouth and tongue that spoke of all these many deeds was, together with the great George of Mats'q'veri, also the blessed father Serapion.
Therefore all these miracles and deeds, which he had seen before his episcopate and afterward, were told to me by that truthful mouth. I mean George of Mats'q'veri.

He told me how the palm branch grew green again, and how he healed that proud and arrogant tongue that had been led astray by the wiles of the devil, for he had been an eyewitness of all of these things.
But now let our account return to the words we began earlier, in their proper order.
And when those disturbances had been calmed, the prosperity of that monastery grew day by day.
And his brother John also came again and again, received his blessing, and learned from him everything that was lacking in the monastery he had built.
And these blessed men laid down this rule for themselves: at the night prayer they would stand with outstretched hands together with the choir of singers.
But when dawn drew near, they would withdraw about a stone's throw away, and in stillness and with tears they would offer their supplications, so that in this too they might be like their King.
And so day by day they increased the talent, so that they might present it, together with its increase, to the Giver of graces.
So, as many years passed, they grew rich in a good old age, and became tender and childlike in divine understanding.
And after this, George's sister Tekla died, and her three sons survived her. Their lordship prospered, and their offspring was blessed, like that of Abraham and Jacob.
But now, brothers, it is right that we listen carefully to what is about to be told.
And when you hear the beginning and the end of this blessed life, you will marvel and glorify God.
For when he drew near to his departure from this world, his passing from sorrow to joy, he called together the community of brothers and said to them:
"Brothers and fathers! I wish to say, as the apostle did:
'The race is finished and I have kept the faith.' I say this not in boasting, but in hope, for from now on the crown of righteousness awaits me,
and not me only, but all who have loved his appearing. For crowns are prepared in this way for those who love him, as he himself says:
'Come to me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest.'
'Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart.' And you, children, learn from the one who says this:
'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and mind, and your neighbor as yourself.' And again he says:
'If you wish people to do something for you, do the same for them.'
'And on these commandments hang all the law and the prophets,' and 'By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.'
"But you, brothers, keep above all the love of God and of your neighbour, as the head of the Law and the Prophets, and pray always,
so that you do not enter into temptation. For prayer brings one near to God; it is the gate of the Kingdom, it joins one to the angels, and it casts down the demons.
For the holy and God-clothed Fathers called prayer a weapon, fasting a wall, and holy tears a bath,
and obedience a martyrdom, which makes a person crowned, without the shedding of blood, together with the disciples who are clothed in the contest."
The holy one told his disciples many things like these with his golden-streaming mouth. And again he said to them:
"Brothers, behold, I am departing in a few days. Seek a father and leader who will be able to shepherd you as children and brothers."
And all of them, filled with tears, wept bitterly, and no one answered him because of their great weeping. When they had recovered themselves, they answered him thus and said:
"Father, since we are being made orphans of our sweet and all-merciful father, we do not know what to answer you."
And the saint said: "Since, children, you tell me nothing, it falls to me, a poor man, to speak myself as is fitting."
Now there was a certain man among the priests, shining with good virtue and sweet in word and deed, named George.
The saint called him and said to him: "O beloved son George, a good lot has fallen to you,
that after me you should shepherd this flock of Christ well, as a soul-loving father; and, as befits children who love their father, they will follow your voice."
When George heard these words, he said, filled with tears:
"It is heavy, O holy one, to lay upon my shoulders a burden so hard to bear. I beg you to forgive me and not to command me again."
But the saint said to him: "Not I, but Christ commands you through me."
And with this word he confirmed him in the leadership of those brothers, at which they all rejoiced, for the whole community regarded him as being like the saint.
And he entrusted his flock to George, and appointed all the officers of the church, as many as were needed.
And he set the community in order with a divine and very beautiful arrangement. Then, on the seventh day after all these things, he fell somewhat ill and lay down on his bed.
But on the fifth day he rose up as though he had become young again, went to the holy sanctuary, and approached the holy altar table and the life-giving icon of Christ's incarnation.

And he gave orders that they should give him communion of the Body and Blood of Christ. And he sealed himself with the Lord's cross, greeted each one of the multitude of the brothers, and said to them:
"Pray for me, brothers, and be saved, for from now on you will not see me again in this world." And he went away and reached his bed at the sixth hour.
And at the ninth hour he committed his soul into the hands of God, for whom he had always longed.
And the fathers of the lavra mourned him not a little, as was fitting, and with tears.
Then his brother John came, for he had been informed by the Spirit, as though carried up by a cloud. And a multitude from the surrounding monasteries and villages gathered.
And the God-clothed George of Atskuri also came with the cross, together with all the ranks of the church.
And let us say this too: the ranks of the angels came, joined with the assembly of all the saints,
as for their fellow camp-dweller and fellow combatant. All of them clapped their hands with joy and carried his most blessed soul up to heaven.
Those in heaven rejoiced and glorified God. Those on earth, freed from diseases and pains by touching that holy body, offered thanks
and worship. With fitting hymns, a multitude of candles and fragrant incense they anointed him and laid him in the tomb
that he had prepared for himself to the east of the altar, so that by seeing it day after day he might remember death, which he always kept before his eyes.
And so they completed the burial rite. At the time of his burial many were healed of many kinds of diseases,
so that all might know that even after death he is alive and labours on behalf of those who entreat him with faith.
But the multitude of his miracles cannot even be grasped by the mind. Still, let us recall some small part of them, and after that let our words fall silent.
The saint's body, which had laboured so much, was still on the bier when, behold, a certain man came who was utterly wasted away.
He was suffering most cruelly from the severity of his pain, for blood was flowing from his private parts, and he was crying out with a terrible voice.
As soon as he arrived, he fervently embraced the saint's bier, and behold, the man became like one dead.
And at once, in the sight of all, his genital member expelled two stones of astonishing size.
And the man became completely healthy, as if that affliction had never befallen him. And all who saw it glorified God, who glorifies his saints.
Then at that time a multitude of people with various illnesses came, and all were healed and glorified God.
And after his burial and his being covered with earth, up to this very day the signs and powers worked through him upon each of the sick are beyond comprehension,
and human speech cannot express or record all the miracles that trustworthy men have recounted to us under oath.
But how shall we tell your love what has been seen and heard in these times of ours?
For the grace of his relics gushes forth ungrudgingly for those who entreat him with faith, and this is accomplished continually to the glory of God.
And now let us recall what grace of prophecy he had been made worthy of.
For behold, the narrative is about to recall the saying he spoke to his brother John:
"In time to come a very beautiful church will be built on this hill." And behold, the time of the prophecy arrived, for while he was still alive,
this saint was beloved by all and was a friend and teacher to all. Because of this, a certain wholly unknown man became this saint's disciple.
The man came from a small place called the village of Dzarghva. Day after day he would come and say to the saint:
"Bless me, father, with your holy hand, and join me to your holy community."
But for a time the saint held him back, so that the marvel would become all the more evident through his remaining a layman.
And he said to him: "Bless me, father, and accept a small eulogia, and spend it on the building of the monastery."
But he again told him to wait, and said that the time itself would come for him to become a monk, and that the eulogia you have prepared would be of great use then.
And when the time came and the saint passed away, the third day after his death arrived, and the saint was laid in the tomb mentioned earlier,
which he himself had built on the east side of the sanctuary, directly facing the window. And that man came, as we said,
on the third day after his death, and wept greatly, and remonstrated with the saint as though he were alive, because he had not been tonsured by his hand. For this reason he said:
"He will not leave the tomb until he has become a monk and has also laid that eulogia at the place of his burial."
And since that man was so fervent, the abbot ordered the keepers of the church to bring scissors and a cowl and to tonsure the man.
And they quickly did as they were told: they tonsured the man and performed over him the whole rite of the monks.
And when he went away and they saw him dressed in unfamiliar clothing, they wanted him to be a layman again.
And when they could not make him obey, they told this to his lord, because that man was useful to him and was a runner on long journeys.
And when the man realized that they would not leave him free to do as he wished, he took that eulogia and as much as he could from his house, and fled.
So they pursued him, but with the help of the saint they did not overtake him.
And when the man went in, [fearing that?] they would seize him and take away what he had, the man went straight to the window of the church and threw in what he had, tied up in a handkerchief.
And so, when the pursuers could do nothing, they begged the superior George
to open the doors of the church, so that they might venerate the saint and also see the eulogia that the man had offered.
O divine providence! This happened so that all might know that even after his death the saint has the power to do whatever he wishes.
And when the doors were opened, they entered the holy church and went up into the sanctuary. They searched for what had clearly fallen in, in plain sight of all, but they could no longer find it,
and fear and amazement seized them all, and they glorified God.
And when many years had passed and the superior George died, a certain Michael was appointed in his place, whom George had instructed:
"Begin building the church according to the command of Father Serapion, and do not worry about the expenses, for the saint made known to me in a vision that the eulogia
which that man brought is buried beneath the cross that stood at the saint's head. Take it up and give it to all the workers,
and make that good man steward of everything, just as under me he also managed all the necessary services of the monastery."
And under this Michael they began the church that the saint had designed beforehand, on the fourth of the month of June, a Thursday,
for by command of the lords, Michael summoned a man famed for his craftsmanship from the land of the Greeks, from a place called Khupati.
He had as his assistant a mason named Shuartqleli.
These two were both the masters and instructors of the many workmen. And since Father Michael knew of it through what had been revealed to Father George,
he went looking for that blessing-gift. The priests went with the Gospel, candles and censers, and the man who had received that blessing-gift went with them.
When they had read the Gospel of John, from its beginning, "In the beginning was the Word," they knelt down and prayed to Saint Serapion.
Then they took down that cross for him, as had been revealed to Father George. O, your wonders, Christ!
For the seal was found completely undisturbed. When that man saw it, he was amazed.
And all gave thanks to God and to the holy Serapion. Then they asked that man how much gold there was and what kind it was. And he said to them:
"That gold is of wrought, pure gold, stamped with the image of the former kings. In number there were three hundred and five drachmas in this sealed bundle."
When they untied the cloth it had been wrapped in, it was found to be just as that man had said before. And they began to build eagerly.
They made that man overseer of the masons, and they also entrusted him with the stewardship of the brothers. In this way the building of the church went forward.
So from the foundation and the first courses, that man provided for all the workmen, apart from their food.
When it had been built, with its piers [?], up to the windows, that man's gold ran out. At that spot he proclaims in a carving:
"Here my money ran out, where I stand, behold, carrying the cross of Christ."
When it had been finished up to the window, they portrayed Michael himself, together with those two masons, above the eastern window.
And the saint's grace always supplied the expenses, for the things they needed flowed in like a river.
During Michael's time as abbot it was built up to the springing of the vault [?]. Then he left this life and departed to the Lord.
After this a certain priest named Paul was appointed as his successor. All the people bore witness to his good character.
This Paul completed the church and adorned it with every kind of adornment.
They set up in it an icon of the Transfiguration, and during Paul's time as abbot they consecrated the church with every blessing.
That man who had received the blessing-gift also departed to the Lord, full of years in a good old age. Let this be enough on this subject.
After this, let us record one more thing and so bring our account to a close. Basil himself, who wrote this Life of the saint, writes and says:
"I, Basil, nephew of Saint Serapion and the least of all monks,
came to his holy monastery some time after his death. I saw that all his works were very splendid and fine, and I was delighted and rejoiced.
When I saw his tomb in a hidden place, where all the sick received healing day after day,
for this reason, by order of the lords, I took the task in hand. I prepared a stone sarcophagus and opened his tomb, and a fragrance came out of it beyond words.
We were all filled with grace, and we glorified God for the wonders worked at that time. For many sick people, when they touched his holy bones,
Many diseases were cured, and the people went home rejoicing and glorified God, the God of wonders.
And with a multitude of candles and the grace of the chanters we laid him in a new reliquary,
and over it we set up a cross in the splendid side chapel of the new church, named for the Forerunner. We appointed one of the priests to offer the Lord's sacrifice in it.
We established the commemoration of this saint, with chanting and spiritual praise, an all-night vigil and a festal celebration, on the twenty-ninth of October,

and afterward, at the time of that liturgy, along with the spiritual feast, there was to be rejoicing with bodily food, richly and abundantly, so that rejoicing in both ways we may glorify God, who glorifies his saints."
But let us tell one more of his miracles, and then make for the haven of quiet silence.
For as soon as the saint's reliquary had been set in place and chanting was on everyone's lips, behold, a man arrived
whose right eye had been ailing for a long time, for it had completely lost its light.
The severe pain made plain that the one eye was blind. And when we all saw him, we all felt pity for him.
The man was from a village called Bobgha. And when he arrived, he fell down before the saint's reliquary.
And we all saw a great wonder, for the man was instantly found completely healed.
And we all glorified God, who ever works powers and miracles day after day at his saint's reliquary.
After this Basil received the office of abbot. For some time he labored well in that place, which his paternal uncle had built up by his labors.
But we, poor and unlearned as we are, turn our words to you, O father of fathers, great ascetic above all, [asking that] as you were to us before, so you may be hereafter.

Now too, never forget us, the weak and unworthy who are called your children, and do not turn away from us, because of the multitude of our sins, your face, which is ever ready to intercede and labor for us.
What praise can we offer you, when the brilliant progress of your life is beyond human nature?
Therefore we offer you the words about your own ascetic labors, as I fall before you in supplication, so that by your intercession you may bring relief for our transgressions,
O companion of the angels, faithful servant of the Holy Trinity, who multiplied a hundredfold the talent entrusted to you, O healer of the weak,
helper of the afflicted, haven of the storm-tossed, wealth of the poor, comforter of strangers and travelers, adornment of ascetics,
chosen one among monks, boast of the fathers, great luminary among abbots, and calm haven for all who flee to you,
teacher of divine zeal to the obedient, glory of the fathers, and, to put it briefly, O you who are worthy of every good name and deed,
accept from me these word-pictures of your virtues, spoken by unworthy lips. And since you are a servant of God the Word,
imitate Christ the King, who accepted the widow's mites, and do not turn away the alabaster jar of unworthy lips, just as Christ did not turn away the harlot's,
and make your dwelling with us, O holy one, as the Lord did in the house of Zacchaeus, and by your prayer deliver us from all the schemes of the enemy,
And just as in this world we have been called disciples of your holy teaching, so also make us partakers hereafter, on that last day, in the glorious coming of the King,
so that we, these unworthy disciples of yours, may stand near you with all the saints at the right hand of the Lord and God, O thrice-blessed holy father Serapion,
through the intercession of the holy Mother of God, and through the grace and prayers of you and of the holy apostles, prophets and martyrs, and of the all-praised bishops and fathers,
so that we, these unworthy ones, may be made worthy to hear that voice of the Easter feast together with the holy angels, who glorify the consubstantial Trinity with the thrice-holy hymn,
to whom is due all glory, honor and worship, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
